title: DDoS Mitigation
description: Understand Layer 3/4 volumetric attacks vs Layer 7 application attacks, Anycast scrubbing, WAF rules, and how Cloudflare's architecture stopped GitHub's record 1.35 Tbps DDoS attack.

segments.text: In 2018, GitHub was hit with 1.35 terabits per second of traffic — the largest DDoS attack recorded at the time. That's equivalent to streaming two hundred seventy thousand HD videos simultaneously, all aimed at one target. It was mitigated in under twenty minutes. Understanding how requires knowing the attack layers.

Layer 3/4 volumetric attacks flood your network with raw traffic. SYN floods, UDP amplification, DNS amplification. The attacker uses open DNS resolvers as amplifiers — sends a tiny query with your IP as the source, and the resolver sends a huge response to you. Amplification factors of fifty to seventy times are common.

Layer 7 application attacks are sneakier. They look like legitimate traffic — HTTP GET requests, API calls, login attempts. Slowloris holds connections open with partial headers, exhausting your server's connection pool with minimal bandwidth. These are harder to detect because each individual request looks normal.

Anycast is the foundation of DDoS mitigation. The same IP address is announced from multiple data centers worldwide. Attack traffic gets distributed across all locations based on BGP routing — each scrubbing center handles a fraction of the total attack. Cloudflare operates over three hundred points of presence, absorbing attacks across their entire network.

Scrubbing centers separate clean traffic from attack traffic. They use pattern matching, rate limiting, and behavioral analysis. Legitimate traffic is forwarded to your origin. Attack traffic is dropped. The key metric is time-to-mitigation — Cloudflare aims for under ten seconds for known attack patterns and under three minutes for novel attacks.

You're under a Layer 7 DDoS attack. The requests look identical to legitimate user traffic — same headers, same patterns, coming from residential IP addresses. How would you distinguish attack traffic from real users?
segments.thought_prompt: How do you filter Layer 7 DDoS traffic that looks identical to legitimate requests?

segments.text: Web Application Firewalls inspect HTTP traffic and apply rules. Rate limiting is your first defense — cap requests per IP per second. WAF rules can block known attack patterns, geographic regions, or suspicious user agents. But static rules are a cat-and-mouse game. Modern WAFs use machine learning to detect anomalous request patterns.

Rate limiting as DDoS defense needs to be multi-layered. Per-IP limits catch simple attacks. Per-endpoint limits protect expensive operations like search or login. Adaptive rate limiting raises thresholds during normal traffic and lowers them during attacks. Always return 429 with a Retry-After header for legitimate clients caught in the crossfire.

Cloudflare's architecture uses every server in every data center for DDoS mitigation — no dedicated scrubbing boxes. They process over sixty-one million HTTP requests per second across their network. Each server runs the same software stack, using XDP and eBPF in the Linux kernel for line-rate packet filtering before traffic reaches userspace.

You're designing DDoS protection for a financial API that must maintain sub-hundred-millisecond latency. You can't afford to route all traffic through an external scrubbing service. What's your architecture?
segments.thought_prompt: Design DDoS protection for a latency-sensitive financial API without external traffic routing.

segments.text: DDoS mitigation is a layered defense: Anycast to distribute volumetric attacks, scrubbing centers to filter traffic, WAF rules for application-layer protection, and rate limiting as the final guardrail. The GitHub attack was mitigated because Akamai's Anycast network absorbed the traffic across global PoPs. Design your system to survive attacks, not just detect them.
